title: Equipment Lease vs Loan in Canada: Which Costs Less?
excerpt: A loan usually costs less over the life of the equipment; a lease needs less cash up front. A $100,000 five-year example in CAD, the RATE formula for leases, and CRA tax rules.
content:
An equipment loan usually costs less over the life of the equipment, and you own it from day one. A lease usually needs less cash up front and makes upgrades easier, but you pay for that flexibility. In our $100,000 example, a $1 buyout lease costs about $7,200 more than a loan over five years.

Below: how leases and loans differ, a five-year cost comparison in CAD, how to find the interest rate hidden in a lease payment, how the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) treats each one, and when leasing still wins.

Short answer

Choose a loan for equipment you will keep for many years, such as machinery or trucks. Choose a lease for equipment that goes out of date fast, such as computers, or when protecting cash matters more than total cost. Before you sign either, compare the total cost over the full term, not the monthly payment.

What is the difference between an equipment lease and an equipment loan?

With a loan, your business buys the equipment and owns it. The lender usually registers a security interest on it and can seize it if you stop paying. With a lease, the leasing company owns the equipment and you pay to use it for a set term.

Leases in Canada come in two common shapes. A lease-to-own lease (often called a $1 or $10 buyout lease) is built so you own the equipment at the end for a token amount. A fair market value (FMV) lease has lower payments, because the lessor keeps the residual value. At the end, you return the equipment, renew, or buy it at its market value.

FeatureEquipment loanEquipment lease
Who owns the equipmentYour business, from day oneThe lessor, until you exercise a buyout
Cash at signingOften a down payment; some lenders finance 100% or moreOften first and last payment only
Total cost over the termUsually lowerUsually higher, especially with a buyout
Main tax deductionCapital cost allowance (CCA) plus interestLease payments, as you incur them
GST/HSTOn the full price at purchaseOn each lease payment
Paying off earlyOften possible, sometimes with a penaltyOften not allowed, or costly
UpgradingSell or trade in what you ownReturn it and lease newer equipment
Used equipmentWidely financedMostly offered on new equipment

The last row matters more than it looks. BDC notes that leasing is usually offered only for new equipment, while buying gives you more options for used or refurbished gear. Our guide to financing used vs new equipment covers what lenders look for in each case.

Which costs less over five years: a lease or a loan?

In our example, the loan costs less than a lease you keep, and the FMV lease costs the least only if you hand the equipment back. The table uses a $100,000 machine, a 60-month term, and illustrative rates of 9% for the loan and 11% built into the leases. They show the math; they are not quotes from a real lender.

$100,000 of equipment, 60 monthsLoan$1 buyout leaseFMV lease (20% residual)
Cash at signing$10,000 down paymentAbout $4,309 (first and last payment)About $3,811 (first and last payment)
Monthly paymentAbout $1,868About $2,154About $1,905
Total paid over 5 yearsAbout $122,095About $129,270 (with the $1)About $114,316
What you have at the endThe equipmentThe equipmentNothing, unless you buy it
Cost to keep it at the end$0$1Market value (assumed $20,000)
Total cost to own itAbout $122,095About $129,270About $134,316

Three things stand out. The loan needs the most cash at signing, but costs about $7,200 less than the $1 buyout lease. The FMV lease has a lower payment than the buyout lease, but becomes the most expensive way to own the machine if you buy it at the end. And the FMV lease only "wins" if you truly want to return the equipment after five years.

Real offers can flip this result. Manufacturer finance companies sometimes subsidize leases on new equipment, and BDC notes their deals on new equipment can be hard to beat. That is why you should convert every offer to a rate before comparing.

How do you find the interest rate inside a lease payment?

Use a spreadsheet RATE function with the payment, the term, the equipment price and the buyout amount. Lease quotes often show only a monthly payment, so this is the only way to compare them with a loan rate.

Formula

In Excel or Google Sheets: =RATE(months, -payment, price, -buyout, 1) × 12. The final 1 tells the sheet that payments are made at the start of each month, as most leases are. For the FMV lease above: =RATE(60, -1905.26, 100000, -20000, 1) × 12 returns 11%. Use the price you would pay in cash, after any discount, or the rate will look lower than it is.

Then compare it with the loan rate, and add the fees to both sides. Documentation fees, registration fees and end-of-lease charges all count. Our article on the fees behind a business loan lists the ones to ask about.

How are lease payments and loan payments taxed in Canada?

With a lease, you generally deduct the lease payments for property you use in your business. With a loan, you cannot deduct the price of the equipment; you claim capital cost allowance (CCA) on it each year, plus the interest you pay.

CCA rates depend on the asset class. For example, most general equipment is in Class 8 (20%), motor vehicles in Class 10 (30%), and computers in Class 50 (55%). Federal measures enacted in March 2026 make the first-year CCA claim larger for eligible property acquired after 2024 and available for use before 2030. For most classes it is three times the normal first-year amount, and manufacturing or processing machinery can be written off in full in the first year.

In our example, if the $100,000 machine were Class 8 equipment that qualifies, the loan's first-year deductions would be about $30,000 of CCA plus about $7,500 of interest. The FMV lease would give about $22,900 of lease payments in year one, plus later deductions as each payment comes due. Over the full term, the totals even out more than the first year suggests, because a bigger CCA claim now means smaller claims later.

A few rules change the math:

  • Passenger vehicles. For leases signed in 2026, deductible lease costs are capped at $1,100 a month before tax. If you buy, the CCA cost limit for a Class 10.1 passenger vehicle is $39,000 before tax.
  • The lease-as-purchase election. If the lessor agrees, you can file Form T2145 to treat a lease as a purchase with a loan. You then claim CCA and the interest portion instead of the payments. The leased property must be worth more than $25,000 in total, and some property, such as highway freight trucks, is excluded.
  • GST/HST. On a lease, GST/HST is charged on each payment, and a registrant can claim input tax credits as each payment comes due. On a purchase, you pay it on the full price up front; a registrant can then claim it back as an input tax credit.

Tax rules depend on your structure and the exact contract, especially for lease-to-own deals. Confirm the treatment with your accountant before you choose.

When should you lease equipment instead of buying it?

Lease when flexibility or cash on hand is worth more to you than the lowest total cost. These signs point toward a lease:

  • The equipment goes out of date in two to four years, such as computers, point-of-sale systems or other technology that is updated often.
  • You want to upgrade at the end of the term without having to sell old equipment.
  • Cash is tight, and a down payment would leave too little for payroll, inventory or slow months.
  • The lessor handles maintenance or service, and that is worth paying for.
  • A manufacturer is offering a subsidized lease rate that beats your loan rate, once you convert it with RATE.

A loan is usually the better choice for equipment you will use for many years, such as production machinery, trailers or construction gear. It is also the way to finance used equipment, and it lets you pay off early if cash comes in. BDC's Equipment Loan, for example, can cover up to 125% of the purchase price, to include shipping, installation and training. It also offers up to 12 years to repay and the option to postpone principal for up to 24 months.

If your bank or credit union is involved, ask about the Canada Small Business Financing Program. It can back term loans of up to $500,000 for equipment and leasehold improvements, with terms of up to 15 years. Our comparison of CSBFP vs BDC loans explains which one fits which business. Frequently asked questions

Is it cheaper to lease or buy equipment in Canada?

Buying with a loan is usually cheaper over the life of the equipment, especially if you keep it for many years. Leasing usually costs less at signing and can cost less in total only if you return the equipment at the end, or if the lessor offers a subsidized rate.

Are equipment lease payments 100% tax deductible?

Lease payments for property used in your business are generally deductible, in the proportion the property is used to earn business income. Passenger vehicles are capped at $1,100 a month before tax for leases signed in 2026. Confirm lease-to-own contracts with your accountant.

What is the difference between a $1 buyout lease and an FMV lease?

A $1 buyout lease is designed so you own the equipment for a token amount at the end, so the payments are higher. An FMV lease has lower payments, but you must pay the market value at the end if you want to keep the equipment.

Can I lease used equipment?

Sometimes, but it is less common. Leasing is mostly offered on new equipment, while loans are widely available for used and refurbished equipment. BDC notes that vendor finance companies often charge higher rates and finance a smaller share of used equipment.

Can I pay off an equipment lease early?

Often not without a cost. Many leases do not allow early payoff, or require you to pay most of the remaining payments. Loans are usually more flexible. Ask for early payoff terms in writing before you sign either one.
